text: May 1935. Two towers standing in open sea, seven hundred and forty-six feet each, and most of a mile of nothing between them.
In one Army photograph from that spring a flying boat crosses the gap, straight through the air where the roadway was going to go.
By May 1936 the cables were spun. Six months and nine days, ahead of schedule. Still no deck. Two curves of wire hanging over the strait.

The name on the job was Joseph Strauss. He had been selling this bridge to northern California since 1921, civic group by civic group. Higher property values. More tourists. A city that would finally stop growing slower than the country around it.
And the thing he was selling looked nothing like the thing in that photograph.
Strauss drew a hybrid. A stiff cantilever arm thrown out from each shore, and a suspended span hung in the middle.
There are renderings of it in a 1933 trade magazine. A plain latticed post for a tower. None of the fluting. A heavy braced arch springing off the San Francisco side.
The public hated it. They called it the rat-trap.
Strauss had built something like four hundred drawbridges by then. He had never built a suspension bridge in his life.
The arithmetic was done by Charles Ellis. A professor, brought in to run the numbers, and he ran thousands of them by hand. He wrote the specifications too.
He worked alongside Leon Moisseiff, who had designed the Manhattan Bridge and worked out the deflection theory that lets a span go that long and stay that thin.
Between them they threw the hybrid out. What they put up instead was pure suspension: the longest main span in the world, and it held that for twenty-seven years.
They moved the Marin pier two hundred feet closer to shore to bring the foundation cost down. That is the bridge everybody photographs.
In late 1931, Strauss dismissed him. He said Ellis was wasting time and money.

text: The bridge opened on the twenty-seventh of May, 1937. The invitation went out over three signatures: a mayor, a fiesta chairman and the district president. No engineer is named on it anywhere.
Bolted to the orange steel there is a bronze tablet with the whole project cast into it in raised capitals.
Officers. Directors, county by county. Contractors, by work package. And a column headed ENGINEERING STAFF, twelve names deep, with Joseph Strauss at the head of it.
He is on that tablet twice. Charles Ellis is not on it at all.
style: No emphasis on the second sentence. Let it sit.

text: Four years later they put an eight-foot bronze Strauss at the San Francisco end. Hand at his side. A roll of drawings under his arm.
He had died in 1938, a year after the opening, and his widow paid for it. The plaque on the pedestal calls him the man who built the bridge.
In 2012 the District rebuilt the plaza around him and cast the caption again. This time it calls him the bridge's first chief engineer. A careful phrase. The 1941 plaque had not bothered with one.
Ellis got his in an obituary. He died in 1949, and the notice named him as the designer.
The District took another fifty-eight years to say the same thing in a report of its own. Then, in 2012, it screwed a recognition plaque to the south tower.
That tower already carried a bronze from 1962. It honours the courageous, farsighted men who devised and built this span, and then names fourteen directors and a general manager instead.
The engineering drawings survive. The copy in the Library of Congress is signed by Charles Ellis.
